headline: Amazon devices chief: AI devices will replace apps
summary: Panos Panay envisions a future of ambient computing where AI devices anticipate needs, reducing reliance on traditional apps.
details: Amazon's SVP of Devices, Alexa & Leo, Panos Panay, believes the future of personal computing lies in ambient devices that work in the background, rather than apps that require direct user commands.

Panay explained that current interactions with smartphones are often cumbersome, involving remembering commands. Ambient devices, he suggests, will allow users to stay more present and get more done without constant interaction.
Amazon's new Bee devices, including a wearable band and a credit-card-sized gadget, are designed to passively record audio and note-taking to identify to-dos and insights.

To address privacy concerns, Bee devices process audio in real-time and delete raw recordings. Transcripts are encrypted with user-controlled keys, ensuring that Amazon employees cannot access them unless intentionally shared.
Panay, who previously oversaw Microsoft's Surface devices, emphasized that privacy must be a core design principle for ambient computing products like Bee.
He anticipates a future generation that won't ask for an app to perform a task but will expect devices to understand their needs implicitly.
While not advocating for the complete replacement of smartphones, Panay sees a new category of devices emerging that use sensors to provide intelligence and better understand users.
The ultimate goal is an "intelligence layer" that connects all devices and is genuinely useful to the user, moving beyond a single dominant form factor.
caption:
Amazon's Panos Panay predicts a future where AI devices will make apps obsolete. "I think that transformation is coming," he stated.

Amazon's SVP of Devices, Alexa & Leo, Panos Panay, believes the future of personal computing lies in ambient devices that work in the background, rather than apps that require direct user commands.

Panay explained that current interactions with smartphones are often cumbersome, involving remembering commands. Ambient devices, he suggests, will allow users to stay more present and get more done without constant interaction.

Amazon's new Bee devices, including a wearable band and a credit-card-sized gadget, are designed to passively record audio and note-taking to identify to-dos and insights.

To address privacy concerns, Bee devices process audio in real-time and delete raw recordings. Transcripts are encrypted with user-controlled keys, ensuring that Amazon employees cannot access them unless intentionally shared.

Panay, who previously oversaw Microsoft's Surface devices, emphasized that privacy must be a core design principle for ambient computing products like Bee.

He anticipates a future generation that won't ask for an app to perform a task but will expect devices to understand their needs implicitly.

While not advocating for the complete replacement of smartphones, Panay sees a new category of devices emerging that use sensors to provide intelligence and better understand users.

The ultimate goal is an "intelligence layer" that connects all devices and is genuinely useful to the user, moving beyond a single dominant form factor.
